issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: 'Always plan an escape route before entering a place' implies a persistent current external-danger / entrapment threat style that is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on intrusive sensory memory linked to the child's illness (body parts, darkness, songs; reliving, fragments, present-tense memory). For trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, this strategy is clinically much less coherent than avoidance/sleep delay, and it is not supported by any Threat or Appraisal items. Given the formulation, Triggers and Memory are strongly linked, but this item reflects a different syndrome focus (situational escape/safety behavior) not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes.

vignette: Ravi was a 42-year-old farmer living in a rural community, where the sun rose early and set late, but his days had grown darker since his daughter's illness. Two years ago, his six-year-old daughter, Maya, was hospitalized with a severe respiratory infection that escalated to a life-threatening situation. Ravi could still recall the frantic rush to the emergency room, the sterile smell of antiseptic, and the piercing sounds of the machines that monitored Maya's fragile state. The helplessness he felt in those moments haunted him, and now he found himself tormented by triggers that brought the past crashing into his present. Each time a trigger struck him, it deepened his sense of helplessness, leading him to avoid sleep altogether, as he believed that staying awake was the only way to escape the memories that haunted him. The overwhelming nature of these triggers compelled him to develop maladaptive strategies, like staying awake late into the night, convinced that the longer he remained conscious, the less likely he was to re-experience the terrifying memories that lurked just beneath the surface of his mind. Each time a trigger arose, the memories of that hospital room would flood back, leading him to stay awake longer, as he believed that if he kept himself busy and alert, he could prevent those memories from resurfacing. Certain songs played on the radio would transport him back to that hospital room; the upbeat melodies felt discordant against the backdrop of fear he had experienced. Even the sight of specific body parts - a frail hand or a small foot - would send him spiraling, reminding him of the frailty of life and the terror of losing his daughter. These triggers had led Ravi to develop a series of maladaptive strategies. At night, as darkness enveloped his home, he would lie awake and avoid sleep, fearing that the night would bring back the memories he desperately wanted to escape. He had come to believe that by delaying sleep until the early hours of the morning, he could somehow ward off the memories that felt all too real. Whenever he did manage to close his eyes, the memories would crash over him; he would relive the terrifying moments as if they were happening in real time. The vividness of these memories would often intensify his anxiety, causing him to jump at the slightest sound, as even the most ordinary moments became fraught with the potential for triggering painful recollections. These vivid recollections would prompt him to stay awake longer, as he believed that by avoiding sleep, he could escape the onslaught of memories that felt so real, each night stretching into a battle against his own mind. The intensity of these memories compelled him to lie awake at night, convinced that if he could just delay sleep, he might keep those memories at bay, even if only for a little longer. In those moments, he felt like he was back in that hospital room, a prisoner to the panic that followed him relentlessly. The sudden fragments of memory would surface without warning, and just as quickly, they would disappear, leaving him breathless and disoriented. In those moments of overwhelming recollection, Ravi felt compelled to stay awake even longer, believing that if he could keep his eyes open, he might prevent another memory from surfacing. Each time a memory resurfaced, it turned ordinary moments into triggers; a frail hand or a small foot would suddenly evoke the terror of watching Maya struggle to breathe, pulling him back into the past with an intensity that took his breath away. These memories would linger in his mind, leaving him hyper-vigilant to the world around him, as he began to associate everyday sights and sounds with the hospital experience, making him feel as though danger lurked everywhere. These memories pushed him to develop maladaptive strategies, such as staying up late to avoid the nighttime quiet that he dreaded, convinced that sleep would only invite those painful recollections. Ravi's avoidance didn't stop with sleepless nights. By isolating himself from social interactions, he inadvertently reinforced his triggers; every missed gathering became a reminder of his daughter's illness, tightening the grip of his memories and creating a world where he felt increasingly isolated and vulnerable. He found himself withdrawing from social interactions, convinced that being around others would only amplify the pain. The embarrassment of having to explain his daughter's illness or the weight of others' expectations felt unbearable. The avoidance spiraled; he began to isolate himself, convinced that the outside world, with its bright lights and laughter, was a dangerous space that threatened to unravel him. His avoidance of social situations only reinforced his triggers, as each time he stepped back from an invitation, he felt the weight of his memories pressing down harder, making him more convinced that he had to stay away. This self-imposed solitude, however, only deepened his despair. In avoiding social gatherings, he inadvertently reinforced the triggers; every missed event became a reminder of his daughter's illness, tightening the grip of his memories and creating a world where he felt increasingly isolated and vulnerable. As he increasingly avoided social interactions, he found that the world outside felt more threatening, and every missed gathering became a reminder of the life he once had, reinforcing his belief that isolation was the only safe option. The more he avoided people, the more he was reminded of the life he once had, filled with laughter and the joyful chaos of family gatherings. The triggers were relentless, and each time he encountered one, it tightened the grip of his memories, bringing them back with a ferocity that left him gasping for air. The memories of that time were inextricably linked to the moments that triggered them. He had come to associate the memories with the triggers that surrounded him; the fear of those memories resurfacing made him hyper-aware of his environment, as he began to see reminders of that hospital room in every frail figure he passed. A simple song on the radio could send him spiraling into a flashback, where he would find himself again in that hospital room, watching helplessly as Maya fought for breath. He had begun to dread the night, realizing that the darkness felt like a harbinger of those memories - a time when he was most vulnerable to their resurgence. Ravi felt trapped in a cycle where the more he tried to avoid the triggers, the more intensely they invaded his life. Each night he spent awake was a stark reminder of his daughter's fragility, and every piece of his memory seemed to carry the weight of that experience with it. Seeking help had become a necessity after a particularly harrowing night when he awoke in a panic, drenched in sweat, convinced that he was once again in the hospital. The fear of losing Maya had become a shadow that loomed over him constantly. He knew he needed to break free from this cycle, to reclaim the life he once had with his family. As he sat in the therapist's office for the first time, Ravi's heart raced with both fear and hope. He was terrified that he might never escape the memories that haunted him, yet he was equally hopeful that with the right support, he could learn to navigate his triggers and begin to heal. Each time he withdrew from social gatherings, he inadvertently reinforced his triggers, as the memories of Maya's illness would resurface with greater intensity, making him even more reluctant to face situations that might remind him of that painful experience. These vivid recollections intensified his need to avoid sleep altogether, as he learned that the only way to fend off the memories was to keep himself busy and awake, ultimately leading him into a vicious cycle of insomnia.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not establish a clear causal relationship between triggers and maladaptive strategies, as it fails to show how triggers specifically lead to the development of these strategies.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: There is no causal connection described between memory and maladaptive strategies; the narrative does not demonstrate how memories influence or result in the use of maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette lacks a causal link from maladaptive strategies back to triggers, missing how the avoidance behaviors might further influence the perception of triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."

vignette_attempts.vignette: Ravi was a 42-year-old farmer living in a rural community, where the sun rose early and set late, but his days had grown darker since his daughter’s illness. Two years ago, his six-year-old daughter, Maya, was hospitalized with a severe respiratory infection that escalated to a life-threatening situation. Ravi could still recall the frantic rush to the emergency room, the sterile smell of antiseptic, and the piercing sounds of the machines that monitored Maya's fragile state. The helplessness he felt in those moments haunted him, and now he found himself tormented by triggers that brought the past crashing into his present. Each time a trigger struck him, it deepened his sense of helplessness, leading him to avoid sleep altogether, as he believed that staying awake was the only way to escape the memories that haunted him. The overwhelming nature of these triggers compelled him to develop maladaptive strategies, like staying awake late into the night, convinced that the longer he remained conscious, the less likely he was to re-experience the terrifying memories that lurked just beneath the surface of his mind. Certain songs played on the radio would transport him back to that hospital room; the upbeat melodies felt discordant against the backdrop of fear he had experienced. Even the sight of specific body parts — a frail hand or a small foot — would send him spiraling, reminding him of the frailty of life and the terror of losing his daughter. These triggers had led Ravi to develop a series of maladaptive strategies. At night, as darkness enveloped his home, he would lie awake and avoid sleep, fearing that the night would bring back the memories he desperately wanted to escape. He had come to believe that by delaying sleep until the early hours of the morning, he could somehow ward off the memories that felt all too real. Whenever he did manage to close his eyes, the memories would crash over him; he would relive the terrifying moments as if they were happening in real time. These vivid recollections would prompt him to stay awake longer, as he believed that by avoiding sleep, he could escape the onslaught of memories that felt so real, each night stretching into a battle against his own mind. The intensity of these memories compelled him to lie awake at night, convinced that if he could just delay sleep, he might keep those memories at bay, even if only for a little longer. In those moments, he felt like he was back in that hospital room, a prisoner to the panic that followed him relentlessly. The sudden fragments of memory would surface without warning, and just as quickly, they would disappear, leaving him breathless and disoriented. In those moments of overwhelming recollection, Ravi felt compelled to stay awake even longer, believing that if he could keep his eyes open, he might prevent another memory from surfacing. Each time a memory resurfaced, it turned ordinary moments into triggers; a frail hand or a small foot would suddenly evoke the terror of watching Maya struggle to breathe, pulling him back into the past with an intensity that took his breath away. These memories pushed him to develop maladaptive strategies, such as staying up late to avoid the nighttime quiet that he dreaded, convinced that sleep would only invite those painful recollections. Ravi's avoidance didn't stop with sleepless nights. He found himself withdrawing from social interactions, convinced that being around others would only amplify the pain. The embarrassment of having to explain his daughter's illness or the weight of others’ expectations felt unbearable. The avoidance spiraled; he began to isolate himself, convinced that the outside world, with its bright lights and laughter, was a dangerous space that threatened to unravel him. His avoidance of social situations only reinforced his triggers, as each time he stepped back from an invitation, he felt the weight of his memories pressing down harder, making him more convinced that he had to stay away. This self-imposed solitude, however, only deepened his despair. In avoiding social gatherings, he inadvertently reinforced the triggers; every missed event became a reminder of his daughter's illness, tightening the grip of his memories and creating a world where he felt increasingly isolated and vulnerable. As he increasingly avoided social interactions, he found that the world outside felt more threatening, and every missed gathering became a reminder of the life he once had, reinforcing his belief that isolation was the only safe option. The more he avoided people, the more he was reminded of the life he once had, filled with laughter and the joyful chaos of family gatherings. The triggers were relentless, and each time he encountered one, it tightened the grip of his memories, bringing them back with a ferocity that left him gasping for air. The memories of that time were inextricably linked to the moments that triggered them. He had come to associate the memories with the triggers that surrounded him; the fear of those memories resurfacing made him hyper-aware of his environment, as he began to see reminders of that hospital room in every frail figure he passed. A simple song on the radio could send him spiraling into a flashback, where he would find himself again in that hospital room, watching helplessly as Maya fought for breath. He had begun to dread the night, realizing that the darkness felt like a harbinger of those memories — a time when he was most vulnerable to their resurgence. Ravi felt trapped in a cycle where the more he tried to avoid the triggers, the more intensely they invaded his life. Each night he spent awake was a stark reminder of his daughter’s fragility, and every piece of his memory seemed to carry the weight of that experience with it. Seeking help had become a necessity after a particularly harrowing night when he awoke in a panic, drenched in sweat, convinced that he was once again in the hospital. The fear of losing Maya had become a shadow that loomed over him constantly. He knew he needed to break free from this cycle, to reclaim the life he once had with his family. As he sat in the therapist’s office for the first time, Ravi's heart raced with both fear and hope. He was terrified that he might never escape the memories that haunted him, yet he was equally hopeful that with the right support, he could learn to navigate his triggers and begin to heal. Each time he withdrew from social gatherings, he inadvertently reinforced his triggers, as the memories of Maya's illness would resurface with greater intensity, making him even more reluctant to face situations that might remind him of that painful experience. These vivid recollections intensified his need to avoid sleep altogether, as he learned that the only way to fend off the memories was to keep himself busy and awake, ultimately leading him into a vicious cycle of insomnia.
